title: Michael Carrick facing Manchester United axe amid review by Jason Wilcox
author: Exclusive by Jamie Jackson
text:
Director of football in discussions with Omar Berrada

Pochettino and Howe on radar as possible replacements

Manchester United are moving towards sacking Michael Carrick, though no final decision has been made by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, who is leading the review after the head coach was given the Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa games to turn results around .

Wilcox has been consulting with Omar Berrada, the chief executive, before a recommendation regarding Carrick is made to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy.

If Carrick is removed, Mauricio Pochettino has emerged as a potential candidate as it is understood the USA head coach is open to the position, while sources indicate that Eddie Howe also remains on the radar of Wilcox too.

The former Newcastle manager is taking a break from the game but would consider the job if offered it. United are in the Premier League relegation zone and have three victories in 15 games in all competitions. Carrick came close to being removed after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October. But after Wilcox and Berrada met the following day at the training ground to discuss his position, Carrick was given the three games until the international break to prove he and the players could reverse a dismal start.

A defeat, a win and a draw in those matches plus the team’s displays in each compounded with the overall run of form has moved Wilcox and Berrada towards a position where they are minded to remove Carrick. There is a growing expectation within the club that he will lose his job.

The final decision is yet to be made, though. When contacted on Monday night by the Guardian the club declined to comment.

In what may prove Carrick’s final three games in charge, United lost 2-0 at Chelsea , beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford and drew 4-4 at home against Villa on Sunday. In each game United were uneven. At Chelsea, Carrick’s side impressed in the first half but failed to convert chances before conceding twice after the interval, the second from a penalty after Lisandro Martínez was sent off.

In the Roma victory they were 2-0 behind in a poor opening 45 minutes before three goals in a rousing second one. On Sunday United twice trailed by two goals and entered added time 4-2 down, strikes from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu rescuing a point.

After the Roma game Carrick urged his team to build momentum but within four minutes against Villa they were 2-0 down, continuing a pattern of conceding very early. In the 4-1 defeat at Como > last month, Nico Paz scored after two minutes. This followed Pablo Barrios’s opener one minute into the 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid > the previous week.

title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
text:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

It think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended , but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

title: 'My lifelong dream has come true' - Rising gravel stars carve close victories at Iceman Cometh against former winners Alexey Vermeulen, Deanna Mayles
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Up-and-coming gravel racers Samanth Johnson , 22, and Kyan Olshove, 24, powered to elite titles at Iceman Cometh Challenge on Saturday, both holding off past champions in sprint finishes.

Olshove claimed the top step of his home race on his sixth attempt. The Traverse City native was overcome at the finish, posting 1:32:57 after 31 miles, which was one second faster than his Michigan rival, Alexey Vermeulen .

"Still can't believe this is real… Thank you to everyone who made it possible. My life long dream has come true. It means everything to me," Olshove, who debuted this year in the Life Time Grand Prix, posted to Instagram.

Vermeulen has won the Michigan race three times, most recently in 2023 when he held off 10 riders in a final sprint, including Olshove, who was third. From a long line of chasers this time, Mika Comaniuk of Quebec out-sprinted Alexander Woodford of Ontario for third.

The route follows forested dirt roads, singletrack, doubletrack, and abandoned railroad lines, using the Vasa trail system, and the race changes the route each year. Sharp hills are prevalent in the final miles, and this time the 700-yard (1km) climb of Icebreaker hill was replaced with the Woodchip climb, shorter but punchier.

Barriers also guarded the dirt incline to the finish line this year, so positioning was critical for the final half-mile effort. The new finish saw the women's field set up for a sprint as well.

Johnson exploded from a reduced pack on the uphill charge to score the women's pro win by one second over 2023 champion Deanna Mayles. Making a first appearance at the 36-year-old mountain bike race, Johnson finished in 1:50:49.

Erin Osbourne led a trailing trio for third place, her fifth consecutive top-five finish, with Crystal Anthony going fourth and Lily-Rose Marois fifth. From another group just a handful of seconds later, Samara Sheppard, Sierra Sims and Jenna Rinehart went sixth through eighth, respectively.

"This year's course was a curveball for all those seasoned. A faster, shorter 'highway' on Vasa directly to Woodchip hill (no icebreaker) and a straight shot to the finish," Mayles wrote on Instagram.

"A group of nearly 15 women in the final miles into the last hills on the course. Not a whole lot of features to break up the big packs of pros sprinting into the finish."

Though it wasn't "mountain bike-y" enough for the veterans, the Milligan University senior switched equipment and rode her gravel bike to seal the day. Johnson completed a season in the U23 field at the Life Time Grand Prix, finishing second to Kylee Hanel at Unbound Gravel 100 and went second in the U23 overall standings. After finishing 11th overall at Big Sugar Gravel, Johnson earned one of two MAAP Future of Off-Road Racing scholarships, which include cash and a spot on the 2027 MAAP PRO.FWD team in 2027.

Olshove raced for the first time in the men's elite field at the Life Time Grand Prix this season, finishing outside the top 20. He performed well outside the series, taking top 10s at Belgian Waffle Ride Arizona and Rule of Three gravel races.

title: Manchester’s soulless content machine football clubs sum up post-imperial Britain | Barney Ronay
author: Barney Ronay
text:
United and City dominate the news cycle with stories so strange and vast they threaten to consume the rest of the league

I n Manchester this weekend it was possible to bookend your Thursday‑to‑Sunday entertainment with two cultural events. First up, a debut screening of the re‑released and uncensored Ken Russell film The Devils at Trafford Odeon. And three days later, three miles down the road, Manchester United versus Aston Villa at Old Trafford.

As expected, one of these events provided a visceral cinematic experience, a deeply disturbing two-hour public meditation on the meaning of faith, blood, fear, power, ritual and the fetishising of objects, climaxing in an orgiastic crowd scene of depraved but undeniably erotic abandon, all acted out on a set in a state of glorious and performative ruin. And the other one was a film with Oliver Reed in it.

By the final whistle that wild 4‑4 draw at Old Trafford felt like a fitting endpoint to the opening quarter of the Premier League season. As we head into a 12‑day international break it is customary at this point to take a set of readings, to anatomise the season to date, to offer up a state of the Premier League address.

Five games since the last time we did this, not a great deal has changed. Brighton have maintained their luminous insurgent energy. The headline chart-breakers are Tottenham, up from second‑bottom to 11th. The official Home Office Spurs In Crisis threat level has been downgraded from Definitely In Crisis to Probably In Crisis A Bit Later On. Roberto De Zerbi no longer looks like a doomed and haunted cartoon caterpillar. Instead he looks like a feisty and fun haunted cartoon caterpillar.

Otherwise there has been only one story in town across that autumn segment. And that story is Manchester, and the extraordinary contortions of two contrasting, but deeply conjoined mega-clubs.

Manchester City’s run from October to November kicked off with the guilty verdict on almost all of their financial charges, followed by an adrenal victory at Anfield, and finally a run of three problematic league defeats. United have basically fallen through the floor in the same period: played eight in all comps, won one, and a point off the bottom of the Premier League table.

At the same time both Manchester clubs have dominated the news cycle, inexhaustible content machines, and the source of football-adjacent stories so strange and so vast they threaten to surge up over the seawall and consume the rest of the league.

It is necessary at this point to talk about Michael Carrick and whether he has been sacked yet (current answer: no). It seems likely that this will happen in the current break, once the designated replacement has been lined up. Another Manchester United paradox: only here, in the realm of the mid-season panic-sacking do we suddenly feel ourselves in the hands of a slick and well-practised machine. Stand aside. We’re old hands at this. Leave it to the experts.

But Carrick is of course essentially another bystander to the ongoing reactor core meltdown. He didn’t appoint Michael Carrick. He has done nothing surprising in his role as head coach, simply been the best Michael Carrick he can be, which is a Michael Carrick unqualified for this level of management.

Even the club executives captured by the TV pictures in insinuating close-up every week are essentially bit-part players, useful idiots for the regime: the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who looks every week a bit more like an office clerk trapped inside a hijacked foreign embassy trying to signal desperately with his eyes that he’s close to the edge and can someone in a flak jacket please appear at the fire escape window pretty soon. And the chief executive, Omar Berrada, who personally oversaw the Manchester City commercial sponsorship regime, and surely can’t be allowed to stay in his role at a listed company if the appeal against City’s charges is dismissed.

These are just the visible symptoms, not the cause. This is what happens when you run an institution where it is necessary to appoint people at significant levels who are willing to exist at a compromised level, who feel delighted to have the chance to run this organisation, even badly.

And by now it feels too easy to say the obvious thing. Manchester United have one competent but entirely self-motivated majority owner, for whom this has been a wonderful financial opportunity; and another owner whose only addition to the spectacle is to demonstrate the non‑transferable skills of the average billionaire.

We know this now. United are trapped in a cycle of self‑consumption. It is an ingrained, self-cannibalising decline, like a depressed post‑industrialised city in miniature. All that remains is rust, people and unspent heritage.

But it has also created something extraordinary in the past few weeks. Right now the Old Trafford match‑day atmosphere feels entirely unlike anything else, not just in sport but any other human activity at which you care to point.

The periphery is now enshrined definitively as The Event. Here is a man in sodden navy woollen menswear haunted by strange noises, striding the touchline like King Lear on his way to a golfing weekend. Here is the United crowd clamped together inside a clanky and leaking stadium, gripped by macro‑forces, shouting at the tides of power, a drama of alienation taking place just beyond the white lights around the lip of the stand.

The currents of energy are so mixed and nuanced. Who is cheering what? Where exactly is the love, the fear, the rage directed at this moment? Like all the best human dramas it is both sweeping and bathetic, thousands of human souls in that same shared space, all focused on an abstract idea, the act of faith and memory they identify collectively as Manchester United, while in front of them Harry Maguire trots about like an ageing police horse and Diogo Dalot attempts to play football with his legs on the wrong way round.…

title: Inside a WorldTour pro's off-season: Watching NBA with Remco, much-needed days on the couch, and exhausting wind tunnel tests - Luke Tuckwell's column
author: Luke Tuckwell
text:
If you've scrolled through social media over the past few weeks, you'd have come across countless posts from professional cyclists around the world enjoying their off-seasons and giving followers a small glimpse into what they have been doing. I'm guilty of this too. Posting 20 photos on Instagram of where I've been, what I’ve eaten, and who I’ve been spending my time with. It’s straight to the point. So today I'm going to give a deeper dive into what my off-season looked like, how it’s shaping my 2027 season, and why it was the best off-season I have had to date.

I was one of the lucky pros at the end of this year (admittedly, that depends on how you define lucky) because I finished my season relatively early after a jam-packed neo pro season. The World Championships road race in Montreal was my final event of the 2026 season, and although I didn’t finish, I had a great time with the Australian team. It was a perfect way to close out the year.

As I sat on the flight back to Barcelona, I had a strange feeling inside me, though. I didn’t really want the season to end. It had been so good to me, and I had enjoyed it so much. Being a neo pro was nice too. It gave me the luxury of making mistakes and not having as much pressure on my shoulders at races, and as you move further into your career, more is expected from you as an athlete.

On the other hand, I was completely exhausted. I had 41 race days under my belt before July arrived without having raced the Giro, and rounded off the year by finishing my first Grand Tour at La Vuelta. I ended the season with 67 race days, almost the same as my 2024 and 2025 seasons combined.

Needing time to do absolutely nothing

I was well and truly ready to take some time for myself, sit on the couch for hours on end and enjoy the few weeks of the year when I can truly do whatever pleases me. After a few days at home post-travel back from Montreal, I planned to travel to the Basque Country in northern Spain with my parents and some family friends for a few days. But when the day came to travel, I was still completely exhausted, and all I wanted was to sit on the couch and spend some time in my own apartment.

It was a good decision in the end, because after almost two weeks, when it was time for the ‘planned’ holiday part of my off-season, I already felt completely rested and my body was returning to normality, if that's how you want to call it.

I wasn’t keen on any overseas holidays this year like a lot of my fellow pros do (I have these trips planned in my head for the coming years), but instead I wanted to stay local and avoid yet more air travel. Thankfully, the beautiful Costa Brava in northern Spain is only a three-and-a-half-hour drive from my home in Andorra. So I spent a wonderful, very relaxing few days there with my girlfriend, whose off-season it was too. We both recharged our batteries lying in the early autumn Spanish sun. By now, it had already been close to three weeks without the bike for me, and I was starting to get a bit antsy.

Throughout this time, I tried to exercise to keep me sane, opting for walks or hikes. It felt nice to spend an hour outside every day just following a dirt track and seeing where it took me. I didn’t do any crazy hikes to mountain peaks like others do; I don’t have the required skill level for that. I stuck to what I knew because the last thing I wanted was to call up the team and tell them I can’t walk or start riding again because I'd sprained my ankle…

By this point, the off-season finish line was edging closer and closer, but there were still two big requirements to tick off. First was my team’s annual October medical camp at Red Bull HQ in Austria, a jam-packed two days of tests at the Athlete Performance Centre (APC) followed by commercial shoots, all in preparation for the 2027 season. But the big ticket item of my off-season was still to come. Every year the team sends roughly six riders to Specialized HQ in Morgan Hill, California, for wind tunnel testing. I was fortunate enough to do this twelve months ago when I was still on the Rookies. But this year our trip had some extra flair.

The realities of wind tunnel testing

Alongside my teammates Remco Evenepoel and fellow Aussie Jai Hindley, I jetted off to the USA as part of the first group of riders, and this year we had a little side quest mission in Los Angeles to complete. After the twelve-hour flight from Munich to LA, we had a basketball game lined up that evening, the first NBA game I've watched in my life and a cool introduction to America’s sporting culture. We visited Red Bull’s APC in LA and toured their facilities across the pond. We played beach tennis, visited the Santa Monica Pier, took part in a community ride with Specialized Santa Monica, and carried out a cheeky recon of the potential LA 2028 Olympics ITT course . All in all, I haven’t laughed that much in a long time, and it truly felt like a Year 10 boys' school trip. But we still had the ‘work’ part of the trip to go: the wind tunnel testing at the Specialized WinTunnel.

Without giving too much away, I personally made significant gains on my TT position thanks to all the new pieces of equipment developed by Specialized and the team. I am sure most of the readers of this are also aware of the wind tunnel testing Cyclingnews Labs carries out, but I want to give you an insight into how tough wind tunnel testing actually is on the body.

For context, testing at Specialized is made up of six and a half-minute runs. So every time you change something, even the smallest detail, you complete one full run to gather data, and sometimes you even complete that same run twice to reinforce the findings. My time in the tunnel consisted of two morning sessions which ultimately ran into the early afternoon. On day one, I completed 18 runs, followed by a solid 24 runs the following day (I broke my personal 2025 record of 22 runs, so I was pleased). But the hardest part is consistently holding the extremely aggressive position on the time trial bike again and again and again. You get to the point where you cannot feel your arms anymore, and your back, neck, and shoulders are crying out for a moment of relief. But the pain is temporary; we are here to get faster, so you take down another can of Red Bull and keep going for another few hours.

While you're in the tunnel with 50km/h wind blasting you in the face, all you can think about is how happy you will be once it’s all over, but to be honest, I look back on it with fond memories because it is such a rewarding experience. You can literally see how much faster you are getting with each run, and I can tell you that is a pretty special feeling knowing you are making those gains. I am already looking forward to the next time I get the opportunity to return to the WinTunnel.

So that summarises my off-season. After a long journey back from Morgan Hill back to Andorra, I decided it wasn’t quite enough travelling for me, so I spent another twelve-hour day travelling to visit my girlfriend in Denmark. Yes, she is Danish, so don’t worry we didn’t just come to Denmark in early winter for fun. As I write this, I am ten days back into training and feeling extremely motivated for the new season. I'll spend another two weeks here in Denmark, two weeks back home in Andorra, two weeks in Mallorca for December camp, then travel back to Australia for Christmas and, all being well, I'll start my season at the Tour Down Under again.

Thanks for taking the time to read this column. I hope you enjoyed it, and see you again soon.

title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
text:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.

While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.

"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.

Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.

A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.

Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.

He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.

By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."

The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
text:
Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023.

He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work.

At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked.

She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial.

She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court.

Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.

That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.

In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.

Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.

But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs until September 2023 when he left the Civil Service.

He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of Civil Service databases, such as payroll, every two years to look for anomalies.

On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".

Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.

He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.

He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box.

Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.

He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".

But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system.

However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?

Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.

Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said.

"That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."

There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.

Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.

But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.

In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.

While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.

His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.

Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.

Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.

But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.

In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.

A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.

An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.…

title: 'If I start discussing contracts here, I think I'll go crazy' –Paul Seixas not thinking about future deal as off-season rolls on
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The future of French superstar Paul Seixas remains up in the air as the offseason rolls on, with the 20-year-old's Decathlon CMA CGM contract set to expire at the end of the 2027 season.

Seixas is the brightest rising star in the sport, having won La Flèche Wallonne, Itzulia Basque Country, and Il Lombardia this season while finishing fourth in his debut Tour de France.

Decathlon will be hoping to keep their leader on board well beyond then as he looks to challenge Tadej Pogačar and inherit the Slovenian's crown as the world's most dominant rider, though UAE Team Emirates-XRG are among the teams interested in his signature.

Seixas is currently enjoying his off-season vacation in Asia, taking on the Tour de France Singapore Criterium before heading to its sister event in Saitama. He told that he's putting contract negotiations out of his mind for now, saying he'd "go crazy" if he devoted too much thinking time to the process.

"I'm on vacation right now. If I start discussing contracts here, I think I'll go crazy. I've taken this time to rest, and I figure if I don't think about it for now, things might be clearer when I think about it again. We'll see what I think about it in the future. But for now, I'm giving myself time," Seixas said.

"It’s a vacation, no doubt about it. I’m really enjoying it; I took the break I wanted. Of course, it makes for a busy day or two, but on the other hand, I’m enjoying being away and seeing things that are completely new to me, so it’s cool. The real restart will be on November 20th, a few days after Saitama, which gives me time to rest a bit and readjust. And then it’s back to racing."

Despite not wanting to devote his mental space to thoughts of his future, Seixas acknowledged that it's a fact of life within the sport. He said that he finds speculation over his future as "pointless", however.

"I think it's part of the sport. It's normal that people talk about what's next; it's good, because it means that people are interested in me and want to know where I'm going," he said.

"Personally, though, I sometimes find it a bit pointless. Will I stay? Won't I stay? Right now, there's no certainty. Sometimes I come across articles, things on social media, and it makes me laugh a little because there are things I learn."

Seixas did talk a little about his hopes for his future contract, wherever that may be. Rather than financial considerations occupying the forefront of his mind, he's instead prioritising other things.

"They could offer me the moon. It's a very difficult question for me," he said.

"I'm looking for a feeling, a connection. I want to really feel in sync with this team, with people I like. I think that's the most important thing, ultimately."

FIA boss planning to end age limits for office holders
text:
FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem is planning to end age limits for office holders in motorsport's governing body.

The move, which has been proposed for approval at next month's FIA General Assembly, comes six months after Ben Sulayem ended term limits for those holding leadership posts across the organisation .

The FIA statutes currently rule out anyone over the age of 75 from standing as part of a presidential team.

Critics say it is the latest step by Ben Sulayem as he seeks to ensure he can remain FIA president for life.

The proposal to be put forward to the General Assembly, which has been seen by BBC Sport, argues that "age limits could restrict the number of qualified candidates eligible for election by the competent bodies, in particular individuals whose experience and expertise could be of benefit to the FIA".

An age limit of 70 was imposed in 2023, during Ben Sulayem's first presidential term.

It was a tactic to prevent MotorsportUK boss David Richards from being able to oppose Ben Sulayem at the 2025 presidential election.

At the time, Ben Sulayem, who is 64, argued that this would "enhance governance and accountability within the organisation".

The FIA added that the move to introduce an age limit "reflected the FIA's commitment to maintaining high standards in its leadership and governance structures".

Asked why the body had now changed its position, an FIA spokesperson said: "The proposal to remove age limits for FIA officeholders brings the FIA in line with organisations such as the BBC, whose chairman is 74.

"It was approved by the world councils for submission in line with the process set out in the FIA statutes, and will only take effect if the general assembly votes in favour.

"An age limit excludes candidates solely on the basis of their date of birth, regardless of their experience, expertise, or ability to contribute.

"Ultimately, the competent FIA bodies will retain full authority to elect the officeholders they deem appropriate."

Ben Sulayem's move comes in the context of a European Parliament resolution passed in October 2025 on "the role of EU policies in shaping the European Sport Model" , external .

This includes a clause that "recognises that the autonomy of sport is conditional upon good governance, and calls on international, European, and national sports organisations, as well as stakeholder-representative organisations, to implement the highest standards of governance, integrity and transparency, with appropriate checks and balances to ensure accountability".

A consultation on the topic , external , launched in April 2026, is due to report by the end of this year.

The EU's aim is to "tackle the major challenges facing the sport sector. These include financial sustainability and inequalities, governance issues, volunteering decline and inclusion. The goal is to address these challenges through coordinated action at European level."

The FIA age limit was raised to 75 in 2024 on the basis that it was "modernising the governance of the FIA and ensuring that candidates for the presidency are more aligned with current leadership practices".

Age limits for leaders are not universally common in sports governing bodies. Some implement them to promote renewal, others choose not to, allowing the widest breadth of candidates.

Ben Sulayem was first elected FIA president in 2021 and was re-elected unopposed last December as a consequence of a quirk of the FIA statutes preventing any other candidate from standing.

Three people who wanted to oppose him - including former racing driver Laura Villars and ex-FIA steward Tim Mayer - were blocked from doing so .

Villars is currently engaged in a legal action against Ben Sulayem and the FIA in France challenging its electoral process .

Ben Sulayem's presidency has been marked by a series of controversies on the issues of governance and transparency.

In addition to the removal of term limits, he has introduced statutes reducing accountability and concentrating power in his hands.

And he has fired a series of senior officers who questioned aspects to do with his leadership, including:

the former chief executive officer Natalie Robyn who raised questions about the general governance of the FIA

the head of the audit committee Bertrand Badre, a former head of the World Bank, and the compliance officer who investigated and cleared Ben Sulayem on charges of interfering with two separate aspects of F1 operations

Ben Sulayem's first vice-president for sport, Robert Reid, resigned in April 2025 citing "a fundamental breakdown in governance standards within" the FIA.

At the General Assembly, to be held in Shanghai, Ben Sulayem faces a request by the Ukraine Automobile Federation (FAU) to include on the agenda the issue of violations of the FIA statutes and international sporting code by the Russian Automobile Federation (RAF).

The RAF has opened regional branches in four cities recognised as sovereign areas of Ukraine by the United Nations.

The FAU has already asked the FIA to look into the issue through its court of appeal but has received no response.

The FAU is asking the FIA to suspend the RAF's membership of the international body until it closes all its offices in Ukraine and suspends all activity there.

FAU president Oleksander Feldman said: "Our proposal is fully consistent with the position of the International Olympic Committee regarding the conditions for the participation of Russian athletes in competitions.

"Indeed, such participation became possible specifically on the basis of guarantees provided by the Russian Olympic Committee that it would not conduct activities on the sovereign territory of Ukraine."

title: Relaxed Primož Roglič gets back on the bike for Taiwan Masters Ride despite time and options for finding new team in 2027 running low
author: James Moultrie
text:
While Primož Roglič 's future in cycling remains one of the major unanswered questions ahead of the 2027 season, the Slovenian seems to be unfazed as he's headed to Asia for an appearance at the Taiwan Masters Ride.

Five-time Grand Tour champion Roglic arrived in Taiwan last week as the headliner for the event, which saw him attempt to beat the KOM atop the Wuling Pass, around 200km south of Taipei.

"I think it depends on the feeling or the state you are in, no? Normally it's just fatigue, so as you are tired and the body screams 'please stop', it's just a fight with that inner voice that wants to stop. You're sad, yes, but we'll just continue without hearing it," said Roglič in a promotional video for the Taiwan Masters Ride.

"The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you. I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."

Roglič failed to beat the time, despite the help of Yen Yo Ho and Li Ting Wei, Taiwanese pro riders from Equipo Kern Pharma and Factor Racing, and four others. However, it had reportedly been weeks since the Slovenian had even ridden his bike amid his off-season holidays, and he didn't even bring his own bike with him, instead riding a grey S-Works Tarmac provided to him.

"What an incredible experience to have Primož Roglič take on one of Taiwan’s most beautiful and challenging cycling routes – the East-to-West Wuling Challenge! We also arranged six Taiwanese riders to take turns pacing him and helping him push toward the summit," read an Instagram post from Taiwanese TV anchor and cycling enthusiast Yu-Tien Wei, who also took part in the event.

"Unfortunately, he didn’t break the record this time. (Well, he hadn’t been on the bike for four whole weeks!) But seriously… is it even normal to ride like that after four weeks off the bike?!

"Watching Roglič team up with the Taiwanese riders, taking turns at the front and giving everything they had to push up the mountain, was truly an incredible and inspiring moment. More than just a challenge, it was an unforgettable ride!"

Roglič closed out the 2026 season at Il Lombardia after winning the European time trial title on home roads , having already finished second overall at the Vuelta a España behind Enric Mas in what was a remarkable recovery from being hit by a driver just a month before the start.

He turned 37 in late October, but his results proved he is more than capable of still competing with the very best. With his departure from Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe confirmed earlier in the summer, the hunt for a new team began for Roglič, with Lotto-Intermarché, Pinarello Q36.5, Visma-Lease a Bike, Unibet Rose Rockets and Tudor among the teams rumoured as landing spots for Roglič in 2027.

As the weeks have ticked by into November and closer to the January 1 start of the new racing season, all news surrounding Roglič so far has pointed to him potentially retiring. Just more than a week ago, reported that Lotto and Visma were both not going to happen, and reported on November 4 that Pinarello was looking unlikely.

The speculation surrounding the other teams, too, had gone quiet, and there remains the question of whether Roglič actually wants to continue. In his typical style, he's been vague when answering questions about his future and his desires for a new team.

"It's beautiful, maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it," said Roglič, talking about the European Champion's jersey. "It would be hard to imagine a better end to the championship."

Asked if he will continue to race next year, he said: "I don’t know it yet. We will see. We will see."

But as for whether he wanted to, he replied: "I think so, yes. I think I will still race."

Among active riders in the peloton, only his compatriot Tadej Pogačar has more professional victories than Roglič's 93, and as a four-time Vuelta winner, Giro d'Italia winner, and 22-time Grand Tour stage winner, he represents the old generation against the new wave of young stars, including the likes of Paul Seixas, Isaac del Toro, and Remco Evenepoel.

When he returns home from Taiwan, Roglič should have decisions to make about whether he extends his time in the sport, and whether he can still find the drive and motivation to fight through setbacks and train to compete at the highest level. In 2026, he managed to show the grit he long has, since swapping ski jumping for pro cycling in 2014, but it could end up that his last ride as a professional was on a mountain in Taiwan, not the ideal send-off for one of the modern era's great champions.

Perhaps an early trip into Slovenia on the recently announced Giro route can convince him to come back with a team where he gets the opportunity to properly bow out from the sport on his own terms, and he's also said openly that he wants to return to the Tour de France. The salary will likely be much lower than previous years if he does end up on a new team, but for the moment, retirement looks as likely a possibility as any.

title: Marianne Vos, Lotte Kopecky, Mathieu van der Poel, and Maddy Nutt among stars set to headline Rouleur Live in London
author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
text:
Newly crowned gravel World Champion Marianne Vos , Mathieu van der Poel, Lotte Kopecky and Maddy Nut are among the riders set to headline Rouleur Live in London this week, November 12-14. They will be appearing on stage alongside dozens of other pro cycling talents, including former Tour de France winner Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney.

Vos is widely regarded as the greatest cyclist of all time and, throughout a multi-discipline career spanning 20 years, has won 15 elite world titles, most recently at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Australia, last month.

The three-day event kicks off on Thursday November 12, with a line-up that includes multi-discipline World Champion and three-time winner of the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix, Van der Poel , along with Xaverine Nirere, Niewiadoma-Phinney and partner Taylor Phinney, who recently returned to track racing, and Bradley Wiggins.

The event continues on Friday, November 13, with multi-time track and road World Champion Lotte Kopecky, former World Champion and this year's Tour de France green-jersey winner Mads Pedersen, Ben Healy, and Fabian Cancellara.

The event will conclude on Saturday, November 14, with Vos taking the stage along with Matteo Trentin and gravel specialist Maddy Nutt.

In between, figures from across the sport will attend the event, offering interviews and stage discussions throughout the three days.

Rouleur Live, formerly known as The Rouleur Classic, began in 2015 in London and will be held this year at the Truman Brewery in East London.

Cyclingnews will attend Rouleur Live on an invitation that includes complimentary admission on November 12 and 13. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser of the event or any sponsor.

title: Luxembourg federation lodges official complaint over Marie Schreiber's lost European title, but how can they hope to overturn the decision?
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Luxembourg's cycling federation has officially lodged a complaint in a bid to overturn and reinstate Marie Schreiber as the winner of the European Cyclo-cross title.

Schreiber moved to the left in the two-up sprint to the line with Lucinda Brand (Netherlands), which the jury of UCI commissaires punished with relegation to second place, a decision that has proved controversial .

"Following the women’s race at the European Cyclocross Championships, the FSCL officially filed a complaint with the UEC regarding the jury’s decision," read a statement.

"That is why the FSCL is calling for the race standings to be determined based on the order in which the riders crossed the finish line."

How can the decision actually be appealed?

It is unclear exactly how the FSCL hope to see the decision overturned.

It states it has filed a complaint with the UEC, which organises the European Championships but does not officiate them from a disciplinary point of view. This responsibility, as with all UCI-sanctioned races, falls to the UCI, which applies its rulebook via a jury made up of a number of commissaires.

The UCI's regulations state that infringements relating to race incidents – of which an irregular sprint is one – "are not subject to appeal", except for any fine that has been applied. So the monetary element of a punishment can be disputed but nothing else.

However, the UCI's regulations do leave some wiggle room, later stating that its Disciplinary Commission, which usually deals with more general and more serious issues, can intervene and even overturn a decision.

"The Disciplinary Commission may, at its own initiative or upon request, decide to suspend the implementation of a decision by the Commissaires' Panel," state the UCI regulations.

The Disciplinary Commission can decide on race infringements "which may have an influence on the sporting conduct or the result of an event", such as this one.

However, the same section of the rulebook also states that the Disciplinary Commission can step in "in case the facts were not observed by the Commissaires' Panel or in case all relevant facts for the assessment of the infringement were not available at the time the Commissaires’ Panel disbanded". Only in the latter case will the decision of the Disciplinary Commission replace that of the Commissaires' Panel, according to the rules.

What this suggests is that the Disciplinary Commission steps in when there's been a flaw in the process – not to review a fully-informed judgement made by a commissaire. In this case, the commissaires had all the facts available in the form of the video footage, so it's difficult to see any provision for overturning their decision under this section of the rulebook.

Schreiber and the Luxembourg federation could in theory take legal action and lodge a case with the international Court of Arbitration for Sport, where the UCI is regularly challenged on disciplinary decisions.

'Give Mathieu those five seconds, and you won’t see him again' – Thibau Nys chasing Van der Poel's level of cyclo-cross dominance
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
After scoring his second career European Cyclo-cross Championships title in Zeddam on Sunday, Thibau Nys has said that he aspires to reach the level of Mathieu van der Poel in terms of of not just winning races but dominating them.

The 23-year-old Belgian soloed to glory after leaving behind Joran Wyseure on the final lap of the race, adding the 2026 title to his triumph two years ago.

Nys won five 'cross races last year, including three rounds of the UCI World Cup en route to second place overall in the series – behind Mathieu van der Poel . Now, he's set his sights on being able to convert his strength into the sort of victories Van der Poel has pulled off year after year.

"Just now on the podium, one side of me was happy with what I had already achieved, while the other side was already thinking about what could be better," Nys told after the victory, his second in two starts this season after opening his account with glory in the opening round of the X2O Trofee Koppenbergcross in Oudenaarde.

"Where can I find those extra percentages? Why can’t I just keep riding alone from lap four? In that fourth lap, for example, I unexpectedly gained a small gap, but I immediately felt that I didn’t have the legs to ride at the front by myself for the rest of the race.

"Give Mathieu (van der Poel) those five seconds, and you won’t see him again for the entire race. That is what I want to get to too, although I don’t know if I will ever be able to."

Nys and his Belgian teammate Wyseure were neck-and-neck for much of the race, with Nys unable to go clear at the front before his final-lap effort. In the end, it wasn't a performance reminiscent of Van der Poel's dominant best, but Nys knows what he's aiming for.

"I felt I was really good, but not good enough to just ride ahead on my own for six or seven laps. So it was a bit of a feeling-out process and trying to see where I could create a gap, to then really explode on the last lap," he told .

"Joran was riding at a very high pace and was simply able to maintain a strong tempo. In that respect, he was perhaps slightly stronger than me, but I did have that burst of energy a bit more in the final lap.

"We are really talking about details here, but I did feel, especially in the penultimate lap, that I perhaps had just a little more in reserve on those stairs to strike there in the final lap. And in the end, I managed to do just that."

Nys has put a challenging road racing season blighted by knee surgery behind him to get off to a 100% start on the 'cross bike. Sterner tests lie ahead, including the World Championships at the end of January, as well as battles against Wout van Aert and possibly Van der Poel, who has yet to confirm his cyclo-cross plans for the winter.
